slides.title: Case report
points: Describe one clinically informative case and its lessons
Core concepts, study planning, analysis and interpretation
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple design schematic

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and structure of the design
Plan sampling, measurement and appropriate analysis
Assess bias, interpretation, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and purpose
points: Describe an individual patient's presentation, management and outcome
Identify an unusual or educational observation
Recognize that the design is primarily descriptive and may combine narrative with numerical data

slides.title: Position among research designs
points: Case reports are descriptive observational accounts
They can generate hypotheses or early safety signals
They do not estimate a comparative treatment effect

slides.title: When a case report is appropriate
points: Consider unexpected presentations, diagnostic challenges or novel adverse events
Assess the educational contribution
Avoid novelty claims based only on personal experience

slides.title: Formulating the clinical question
points: Identify what makes the case informative
State the diagnostic or management issue
Define the lesson without assuming causality

slides.title: Assessing novelty and relevance
points: Search for similar published cases and established explanations
Identify the remaining knowledge gap
Distinguish a rare finding from a meaningful contribution

slides.title: Selecting and verifying the case
points: Confirm diagnosis and essential clinical facts
Check original records and dates
Explain uncertainty where evidence is incomplete

slides.title: Illustrative case scenario
points: Hypothetical example: an unexpected ocular adverse event after treatment
Focus on presentation, differential diagnosis and course
Label the example as fictional teaching material

slides.title: Patient information and context
points: Record relevant demographic, medical and exposure history
Include only details needed to understand the case
Protect identifying information

slides.title: Constructing the timeline
points: Sequence symptoms, investigations, treatment and follow-up
Specify meaningful intervals
Make temporal relationships visible without treating sequence as proof of causality

slides.title: Clinical presentation
points: Describe symptoms, signs and initial assessment
Include relevant negative findings
Separate patient reports from observed findings

slides.title: Diagnostic assessment
points: Explain tests, diagnostic criteria and differential diagnoses
Discuss challenges and alternative explanations
Report the basis and uncertainty of the final diagnosis

slides.title: Therapeutic intervention
points: Specify treatment, dose, duration and modifications when relevant
Explain the clinical rationale
Describe co-interventions that may influence outcomes

slides.title: Follow-up and outcomes
points: Report the clinical course and objective measurements
Specify follow-up duration and incomplete observations
Include patient-reported outcomes and adverse events when available

slides.title: Numerical data and images
points: Use laboratory values, imaging or serial measurements with units
Provide clear labels and dates
Obtain appropriate permission for publication of images
slides.visual: Annotated clinical image and measurement table

slides.title: Patient perspective
points: Include the patient's experience where appropriate and available
Distinguish perspective from investigator interpretation
Explain if this information could not be obtained

slides.title: Assessing a suspected adverse reaction
points: Examine timing, biological plausibility and competing causes
Discuss dechallenge or rechallenge only if clinically appropriate and documented
Avoid inferring a population risk from one case

slides.title: Analysis and interpretation
points: Use a structured descriptive account
Compare the case with relevant literature
Avoid p-values or inferential statistics unsupported by the design

slides.title: Worked interpretation example
points: Hypothetical event occurs after exposure and improves after withdrawal
Explain why this supports suspicion but does not prove the cause
Consider underlying disease and other treatments

slides.title: Bias and alternative explanations
points: Consider selective reporting and retrospective reconstruction
Examine diagnostic uncertainty and confounding
Acknowledge that striking cases may be preferentially published

slides.title: Consent and confidentiality
points: Obtain publication consent as required by the journal and local rules
De-identify text and images responsibly
Recognize that unusual details can still reveal identity

slides.title: Reporting with CARE
points: Use CARE to organize the report and check completeness
Present the timeline, diagnostic reasoning and follow-up transparently
Treat reporting guidance as distinct from evidence of validity

slides.title: Strengths, limitations and takeaways
points: A case can reveal a signal or teach clinical reasoning
It cannot establish prevalence or comparative effectiveness
Discuss what a larger study should investigate next

slides.title: References and further reading
points: CARE Case Report Guidelines and checklist. https://www.care-statement.org/downloads
JBI Critical Appraisal Tools. https://jbi.global/critical-appraisal-tools

slides.title: Case series
points: Describe a group of cases with consistent selection and outcome reporting
Core concepts, study planning, analysis and interpretation
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple design schematic

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and structure of the design
Plan sampling, measurement and appropriate analysis
Assess bias, interpretation, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and purpose
points: Describe several patients sharing a condition or clinical feature
Summarize presentations, management and outcomes
Usually provide descriptive evidence without a concurrent comparator

slides.title: Case series versus neighboring designs
points: A case report focuses on one patient
A series describes a group with common features
Exposure-defined follow-up with risk estimation may be better classified as a cohort

slides.title: When a case series fits
points: Use for rare presentations, early experience or safety signals
Assess whether a defined group can answer a descriptive question
Choose a comparative design for treatment-effect estimation

slides.title: Formulating the objective
points: Specify the condition, setting and descriptive outcome
Define the period covered
Avoid wording that assumes an intervention caused the findings

slides.title: Prospective and retrospective collection
points: Prospective collection plans observations before follow-up
Retrospective collection uses existing records
Both require explicit selection and measurement procedures

slides.title: Defining eligible cases
points: Use consistent diagnostic and inclusion criteria
State exclusions and why they matter
Decide whether the unit is a patient, eye, procedure or episode

slides.title: Consecutive and complete inclusion
points: Seek consecutive or complete eligible cases when feasible
Explain how cases were identified
Report omissions and reasons for exclusion

slides.title: Illustrative research scenario
points: Hypothetical example: unusual optic nerve findings at one referral center
Describe all eligible cases over a defined period
Avoid presenting the center's experience as a population frequency

slides.title: Setting and referral pathways
points: Describe service level, catchment and referral patterns
Explain why severe or unusual cases may be overrepresented
Record changes in case ascertainment over time

slides.title: Sample size and scope
points: Justify the available or planned series relative to its objective
Small series yield imprecise summaries
Avoid applying a universal minimum case count

slides.title: Standardizing data extraction
points: Use a predefined form and variable definitions
Verify key fields against source records
Resolve ambiguous or inconsistent documentation

slides.title: Baseline characteristics
points: Describe age, clinical features and relevant comorbidities
Report distributions appropriate to the sample
Keep denominators visible for every summary

slides.title: Clinical presentation and diagnosis
points: Summarize common and differing presentations
Explain diagnostic criteria and verification
Report uncertain diagnoses separately

slides.title: Management and co-interventions
points: Describe treatments and why patients received them
Record variations in management
Recognize confounding by indication if outcomes are compared

slides.title: Outcomes and follow-up
points: Define outcomes and assessment windows
Report follow-up completeness and variation
Distinguish patients with no event from patients with unknown status

slides.title: Descriptive statistical analysis
points: Use counts, proportions and suitable summaries of continuous data
State the denominator for each measure
Avoid unsupported comparative or causal inference

slides.title: Missing data and exclusions
points: Report missingness for key variables
Explain complete-case summaries and their limits
Consider how incomplete records affect the descriptive account

slides.title: Worked descriptive example
points: Hypothetical series includes 12 cases with documented outcomes in 10
If 3 improved, report 3 of 10 among those assessed
Do not silently treat the 2 unknown outcomes as failures or successes

slides.title: Selection and information bias
points: Consider preferential inclusion of severe or successful cases
Examine inconsistent measurement and retrospective coding
Explain how consecutive selection reduces some selection concerns

slides.title: Interpreting proportions and comparisons
points: A proportion within the series describes that selected group
It is not a population incidence estimate without an appropriate population denominator
Exploratory subgroup differences require cautious interpretation

slides.title: Ethics and critical appraisal
points: Protect confidentiality across potentially identifiable cases
Follow applicable approvals and publication consent requirements
Use JBI appraisal questions to examine selection and reporting

slides.title: Reporting, strengths and takeaways
points: Report eligibility, case flow, clinical details and follow-up clearly
Use the series to identify patterns and hypotheses
Discuss what a comparator or larger dataset would add

slides.title: References and further reading
points: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Case Series. https://jbi.global/sites/default/files/2020-07/Checklist_for_Case_Series_0.pdf
CDC Field Epidemiology Manual: Designing and Conducting Analytic Studies in the Field. https://www.cdc.gov/field-epi-manual/php/chapters/design-conduct-analyze-field-studies.html

slides.title: Ecological study
points: Examine exposure and outcome patterns at the group level
Core concepts, study planning, analysis and interpretation
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple design schematic

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and structure of the design
Plan sampling, measurement and appropriate analysis
Assess bias, interpretation, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and unit of analysis
points: Analyze groups such as regions, institutions or time periods
Use aggregate exposure and outcome measures
Keep group-level and individual-level questions distinct

slides.title: Purpose and design scope
points: Describe population patterns or investigate group-level associations
Study policies or contextual exposures
Match conclusions to the level of the data

slides.title: Forms of ecological study
points: Compare multiple groups at one time or one group across time
Consider panel data with groups observed repeatedly
Distinguish observational comparisons from intervention-focused time-series designs

slides.title: When an ecological design fits
points: Use when the exposure operates at group level or only aggregate data exist
Assess data comparability across units
Avoid using aggregate data to answer an individual question without justification

slides.title: Formulating the research question
points: Specify the population units, exposure and outcome
Define the period and association of interest
State whether the aim is contextual or hypothesis-generating

slides.title: Illustrative research problem
points: Hypothetical example: regional deprivation and rates of late glaucoma diagnosis
Compare regions using consistent definitions
Interpret the association at regional level

slides.title: Selecting groups and boundaries
points: Define geographic or organizational units consistently
Explain exclusions and changes in boundaries
Recognize that results can depend on the aggregation scale

slides.title: Exposure measurement
points: Define group means, proportions or policy indicators
Assess whether the measure captures the intended exposure
Consider exposure timing and relevant lag periods

slides.title: Outcome measurement and denominators
points: Use counts, rates or standardized measures suited to the question
Verify population denominators and case definitions
Distinguish prevalence, incidence and service-use outcomes

slides.title: Data sources and linkage
points: Combine compatible registries, census data or administrative sources
Align time periods and geographic identifiers
Document mismatches and source limitations

slides.title: Comparability and standardization
points: Consider age structure, case detection and measurement differences
Use standardization where appropriate to the estimand
Avoid comparing crude rates as if populations were identical

slides.title: Descriptive analysis
points: Summarize group distributions and inspect extreme units
Plot maps or scatterplots with clear scales
Check whether a few groups dominate the pattern

slides.title: Correlation and regression
points: Use methods suited to continuous outcomes, counts or rates
Distinguish correlation from a causal effect
Specify model assumptions and uncertainty

slides.title: Weighting and group size
points: Explain whether groups contribute equally or by population size
Recognize that weighting changes the estimand
Address unstable rates from small populations

slides.title: Confounding at the group level
points: Consider socioeconomic conditions, healthcare access and demographic composition
Select adjustments using a causal rationale
Recognize remaining individual and contextual confounding

slides.title: Ecological fallacy
points: An association between groups need not describe associations within individuals
Illustrate how aggregation can obscure individual relationships
Do not interpret regional deprivation as each patient's exposure

slides.title: Spatial and temporal dependence
points: Nearby regions and repeated measurements may be correlated
Use appropriate models or uncertainty estimates
Consider spillover and time-varying contextual factors

slides.title: Sensitivity analyses
points: Test alternative group definitions, lags and influential-unit exclusions
Examine measurement choices and missing units
Keep analyses tied to the question rather than searching for significance

slides.title: Worked interpretation example
points: Hypothetical scatterplot shows higher late-diagnosis rates in more deprived regions
Discuss group-level access and case-detection explanations
Identify individual data needed to investigate patient-level mechanisms

slides.title: Ethics and data limitations
points: Public aggregate data may still carry disclosure risks in small cells
Follow data-use and local review requirements
Explain underreporting and mismatched source periods

slides.title: Reporting and critical appraisal
points: State the ecological unit, sources, dates and analysis clearly
Report uncertainty and group-level confounding
Make the inference level explicit in the conclusion

slides.title: Strengths, limitations and takeaways
points: Useful for contextual questions and population surveillance
Group-level findings require group-level interpretation
Discuss when multilevel or individual-level follow-up is needed

slides.title: References and further reading
points: Ecological studies: use with caution. Primary methodological article. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3905433/
CDC Field Epidemiology Manual: Designing and Conducting Analytic Studies in the Field. https://www.cdc.gov/field-epi-manual/php/chapters/design-conduct-analyze-field-studies.html

slides.title: Cross-sectional study
points: Measure prevalence or associations in a population at a defined time
Core concepts, study planning, analysis and interpretation
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple design schematic

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and structure of the design
Plan sampling, measurement and appropriate analysis
Assess bias, interpretation, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and purpose
points: Measure variables within a defined time window
Estimate prevalence or examine concurrent associations
Recognize that exposure-outcome timing may be unclear

slides.title: Descriptive and analytical questions
points: Descriptive studies estimate characteristics or burden
Analytical studies compare exposures and outcomes
State the primary aim before choosing sampling and analysis

slides.title: When the design fits
points: Use for burden, service needs or concurrent risk-factor patterns
Plan a coherent observation window
Choose longitudinal designs when change or incidence is central

slides.title: Formulating the research question
points: Specify the population, exposure, outcome and time window
Distinguish a prevalence objective from an association objective
Avoid assuming the exposure preceded the outcome

slides.title: Illustrative research problem
points: Hypothetical example: prevalence of unrecognized glaucoma in a defined adult population
Alternatively examine its association with healthcare access
Keep the estimation and association questions distinct

slides.title: Target and source populations
points: Define whom results are intended to describe
Identify the accessible sampling frame
Explain exclusions and coverage gaps

slides.title: Sampling strategies
points: Compare probability, stratified, cluster and convenience sampling
Align selection with the inference goal
Describe how sampling affects representativeness

slides.title: Eligibility and recruitment
points: Set criteria before selection
Record invitations, eligibility and participation
Prevent recruitment procedures from favoring particular outcomes

slides.title: Sample size for prevalence
points: Use expected prevalence, desired precision and confidence level
Account for design effects and nonresponse where relevant
State the assumptions rather than using a universal sample rule

slides.title: Sample size for associations
points: Base planning on the primary comparison or model
Consider outcome frequency, exposure distribution and confounders
Distinguish available sample size from adequate information

slides.title: Defining exposure and outcome
points: Use validated criteria and consistent measurement windows
Separate current status from recalled past exposure
Specify handling of ambiguous classifications

slides.title: Data collection and quality control
points: Standardize questionnaires, examinations or record extraction
Train assessors and calibrate measurements
Use identical procedures across participant groups

slides.title: Prevalence calculation
points: Divide existing cases by the eligible population assessed
Report the observation window and denominator
Recognize that prevalence reflects disease duration as well as occurrence

slides.title: Descriptive statistics
points: Summarize demographic and clinical characteristics
Use suitable continuous-data summaries and confidence intervals
Describe subgroup denominators transparently

slides.title: Measures of association
points: Consider prevalence ratios, prevalence differences and prevalence odds ratios
Choose an estimand before the model
Do not automatically interpret an odds ratio as a prevalence ratio

slides.title: Regression analysis
points: Use models appropriate to the outcome and selected estimand
Consider modified Poisson or log-binomial models for prevalence ratios
Explain logistic regression estimates prevalence odds ratios

slides.title: Complex survey analysis
points: Use weights, strata and cluster information when required
Account for the sample design in uncertainty estimates
Distinguish weighted population estimates from raw sample summaries

slides.title: Confounding and effect modification
points: Choose adjustments using substantive causal knowledge
Examine meaningful differences across subgroups
Avoid indiscriminate adjustment for mediators or colliders

slides.title: Selection and nonresponse bias
points: Assess coverage gaps and participation patterns
Describe who may be missing from the sample
Weighting cannot fully correct all unobserved differences

slides.title: Temporality and reverse causation
points: Concurrent measurement often cannot establish event order
Disease may alter the measured exposure
Make causal limits explicit even with adjusted regression

slides.title: Worked example and missing data
points: Hypothetical sample has 40 cases among 1,000 participants: prevalence is 4%
Report unavailable examinations separately rather than classifying them as disease-free
Examine sensitivity to nonresponse and missingness

slides.title: Reporting, strengths and takeaways
points: Use the cross-sectional STROBE checklist for reporting
Report prevalence or associations with uncertainty and design limits
Discuss whether longitudinal work is needed to test a temporal hypothesis

slides.title: References and further reading
points: STROBE Statement: reporting observational research. https://www.strobe-statement.org/
CDC Field Epidemiology Manual: Designing and Conducting Analytic Studies in the Field. https://www.cdc.gov/field-epi-manual/php/chapters/design-conduct-analyze-field-studies.html

slides.title: Case-control study
points: Compare prior exposures among cases and controls drawn from a source population
Core concepts, study planning, analysis and interpretation
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple design schematic

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and structure of the design
Plan sampling, measurement and appropriate analysis
Assess bias, interpretation, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and sampling logic
points: Select participants according to outcome status
Compare exposure histories in cases and controls
Understand controls as representing the exposure distribution in the population giving rise to cases

slides.title: When the design fits
points: Use for rare outcomes or outcomes with long induction periods
Study several candidate exposures efficiently
Avoid selecting this design solely because data are retrospective

slides.title: Formulating the question
points: Specify the disease, exposure and source population
Define the relevant exposure window
Ask about the association without assuming causality

slides.title: Illustrative research problem
points: Hypothetical example: obesity history and meningioma diagnosis
Define cases and eligible source-population controls
Assess whether exposure data precede the outcome

slides.title: Source population and time at risk
points: Define the population and period that generated the cases
Controls must have been eligible to become cases
Ensure comparable opportunities for exposure ascertainment

slides.title: Case definition and ascertainment
points: Use consistent and valid diagnostic criteria
Consider incident versus prevalent cases
Describe all case-finding routes and exclusions

slides.title: Selecting controls
points: Choose controls independently of the exposure under study
Match their eligibility to the source population
Avoid convenient controls with different referral or disease pathways

slides.title: Control sampling schemes
points: Compare cumulative, case-cohort and incidence-density sampling
Explain that interpretation depends on how controls are sampled
Avoid treating all case-control odds ratios as identical estimands

slides.title: Number of controls and sample planning
points: Plan around exposure frequency, expected association and precision
Additional controls may improve efficiency with diminishing gains
Account for matching and available cases

slides.title: Matching strategies
points: Use individual or frequency matching only with a clear rationale
Choose variables carefully to avoid overmatching
Explain that matching requires appropriate analysis

slides.title: Exposure ascertainment
points: Use validated records, measurements or interviews
Apply comparable procedures for cases and controls
Choose exposure windows that reduce reverse-causation concerns

slides.title: Data quality and blinding
points: Use standardized instruments and extraction rules
Blind exposure assessors to case status where feasible
Verify uncertain classifications systematically

slides.title: The 2-by-2 table
points: Define exposed and unexposed participants among cases and controls
Label cells and totals consistently
Understand that the sampled case fraction is set by design

slides.title: Calculating the odds ratio
points: With exposed cases a, exposed controls b, unexposed cases c and unexposed controls d, OR is ad divided by bc
Report uncertainty with the estimate
State the exposure comparison clearly

slides.title: Interpreting the odds ratio
points: For cumulative sampling, the OR approximates a risk ratio when the outcome is rare in the source population
Incidence-density sampling can estimate a rate ratio without a rare-outcome assumption
Do not estimate absolute risk from the case fraction

slides.title: Regression and matched analysis
points: Use logistic regression for appropriate unmatched analyses
Consider conditional logistic regression for individually matched sets
Include the matching structure in the analytic plan

slides.title: Confounding and effect modification
points: Select covariates using a causal rationale
Compare crude and adjusted estimates appropriately
Assess clinically meaningful subgroup differences without data dredging

slides.title: Selection bias
points: Examine referral patterns, survival and control participation
Hospital controls may have exposure-related conditions
Explain how selection can distort the exposure contrast

slides.title: Recall and information bias
points: Cases may remember past exposures differently from controls
Records may be incomplete or measured differently
Prefer comparable objective information when feasible

slides.title: Worked example
points: Hypothetical counts are a=40, b=20, c=60 and d=80
OR equals 2.67 after rounding
Interpret the result under the stated sampling scheme and avoid claiming a causal effect

slides.title: Sensitivity analyses and ethics
points: Examine exposure definitions, control sources and missingness
Consider reverse-causation and residual-confounding scenarios
Protect sensitive health records and follow required review procedures

slides.title: Reporting, strengths and takeaways
points: Use the case-control STROBE checklist
Explain case selection, control sampling, matching and exposure timing
Discuss why a valid source population matters more than simply increasing control count

slides.title: References and further reading
points: STROBE Statement: reporting observational research. https://www.strobe-statement.org/
CDC Field Epidemiology Manual: Designing and Conducting Analytic Studies in the Field. https://www.cdc.gov/field-epi-manual/php/chapters/design-conduct-analyze-field-studies.html

slides.title: Cohort study
points: Follow an outcome-free or otherwise defined population over time to compare outcomes
Core concepts, study planning, analysis and interpretation
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple design schematic

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and structure of the design
Plan sampling, measurement and appropriate analysis
Assess bias, interpretation, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and temporal structure
points: Define a population before the outcome assessment period
Classify exposures and follow subsequent outcomes
Align eligibility, exposure assignment and follow-up start

slides.title: Prospective and retrospective cohorts
points: Prospective studies collect future outcomes
Retrospective cohorts reconstruct follow-up from existing records
Both require a coherent time origin and temporal order

slides.title: When the design fits
points: Use for incidence, prognosis and multiple outcomes
Consider feasibility of follow-up and outcome frequency
Recognize resource demands and inefficiency for very rare outcomes

slides.title: Formulating the question
points: Specify population, exposure or treatment, comparator and outcome
Define the follow-up horizon
State whether the aim is descriptive, prognostic or causal

slides.title: Illustrative research problem
points: Hypothetical example: baseline obesity and later meningioma diagnosis
Define an eligible population without the outcome at entry
Assess detection differences and plausible confounders

slides.title: Defining the cohort and time zero
points: Apply eligibility criteria at a consistent index date
Establish baseline outcome status
Avoid using future information to define exposure or entry

slides.title: Selecting the comparison group
points: Use a comparator from a compatible population and period
Check exposure overlap and baseline differences
Define reference categories precisely

slides.title: Exposure measurement
points: Specify baseline, repeated or time-varying exposure
Use valid measurements and meaningful categories
Consider changes in exposure during follow-up

slides.title: Outcome definition and ascertainment
points: Use consistent criteria and ascertainment across groups
Distinguish incident outcomes from historical codes
Consider validation and competing events

slides.title: Follow-up and censoring
points: Define the end of follow-up and censoring rules
Record loss to follow-up and reasons where available
Recognize bias if censoring depends on outcome risk

slides.title: Sample size and event planning
points: Base planning on the primary estimand and expected event frequency
Account for follow-up duration and attrition
A large cohort may still contain few informative events

slides.title: Risk and cumulative incidence
points: Estimate the probability of an outcome over a defined period
Keep numerator, denominator and follow-up horizon aligned
Consider censoring and competing risks where relevant

slides.title: Person-time and incidence rates
points: Sum time contributed while participants remain at risk
Divide events by person-time for an incidence rate
Distinguish a rate from a probability

slides.title: Comparative measures
points: Compare risk ratios, risk differences and rate ratios
Explain absolute and relative interpretations
Do not substitute a hazard ratio for a risk ratio

slides.title: Survival analysis
points: Use Kaplan-Meier estimates when assumptions fit the question
Explain Cox models and proportional-hazards assessment
Recognize competing-risk and time-varying-effect alternatives

slides.title: Confounding control
points: Use design restrictions and prespecified adjustment
Consider propensity methods when justified by the objective
Explain that adjustment cannot remove unmeasured confounding by itself

slides.title: Immortal time and other timing errors
points: Do not assign future survivors to an exposed group from baseline
Align treatment decisions and follow-up start
Consider time-varying exposures or target-trial principles

slides.title: Selection and surveillance bias
points: Assess loss to follow-up, differential testing and coding
More contact with healthcare may increase outcome detection
Explain how selection affects internal and external validity

slides.title: Missing data and sensitivity analyses
points: Describe baseline and follow-up missingness
Choose methods with defensible assumptions
Test alternative exposure, outcome and follow-up definitions

slides.title: Worked comparative example
points: Hypothetical one-year risks are 20 of 200 exposed and 10 of 200 unexposed
Risk ratio is 2.0 and risk difference is 5 percentage points
State that these crude contrasts may reflect confounding

slides.title: Ethics and data stewardship
points: Protect longitudinal records and sensitive exposures
Follow applicable consent or waiver requirements
Specify access, linkage and retention safeguards

slides.title: Reporting, strengths and takeaways
points: Use the cohort STROBE checklist
Report follow-up, events, censoring and adjusted estimates transparently
Discuss the credibility of timing, comparator choice and remaining bias

slides.title: References and further reading
points: STROBE Statement: reporting observational research. https://www.strobe-statement.org/
CDC Field Epidemiology Manual: Designing and Conducting Analytic Studies in the Field. https://www.cdc.gov/field-epi-manual/php/chapters/design-conduct-analyze-field-studies.html

slides.title: Uncontrolled before-and-after study
points: Compare outcomes before and after an intervention in one group
Core concepts, study planning, analysis and interpretation
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple design schematic

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and structure of the design
Plan sampling, measurement and appropriate analysis
Assess bias, interpretation, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and structure
points: Measure outcomes in a group before and after a change
Include no concurrent untreated comparison group
Distinguish paired individual follow-up from repeated samples of a population

slides.title: Purpose and design scope
points: Describe change following implementation
Use for preliminary local assessment or feasibility
Recognize limited ability to attribute change to the intervention

slides.title: When the design fits
points: Consider use when a concurrent comparator is unavailable
Assess whether repeated time-series data could strengthen the design
Explain why randomization or a comparison group was not used

slides.title: Formulating the question
points: Specify intervention, population, outcome and assessment windows
Define the change being estimated
Use wording that distinguishes temporal change from causal benefit

slides.title: Illustrative research problem
points: Hypothetical example: attendance before and after a clinic reminder system
Compare consistent periods and definitions
Consider other changes in clinic access or workload

slides.title: Defining the study population
points: Clarify whether the same individuals are measured twice
Set eligibility consistently at both periods
Record changes in population composition

slides.title: Describing the intervention
points: Specify content, delivery, start date and intensity
Document adaptations and implementation fidelity
Identify co-interventions occurring at the same time

slides.title: Selecting baseline and follow-up windows
points: Choose periods that fit the expected response
Keep seasonal and service differences in view
Avoid choosing the best-looking post-intervention period after examining results

slides.title: Baseline measurement
points: Use reliable measurements before implementation
Record context and initial performance
Consider whether an unusually poor baseline prompted the intervention

slides.title: Outcome measurement consistency
points: Use the same instruments, criteria and denominators across periods
Record changes in coding or data collection
Keep assessment procedures stable where possible

slides.title: Sampling and sample size
points: Plan around the primary change estimate and desired precision
Account for within-person correlation in paired designs
Include attrition and available population counts

slides.title: Paired continuous outcomes
points: Estimate mean or median within-person change as appropriate
Consider paired tests or longitudinal models with suitable assumptions
Avoid treating paired observations as independent

slides.title: Independent pre-post samples
points: Compare group summaries with methods for independent samples
Adjust for relevant composition differences where possible
Explain that adjustment does not create a true counterfactual

slides.title: Binary outcomes and proportions
points: Use paired methods such as McNemar's test for paired binary data when appropriate
Compare independent proportions with suitable methods for independent samples
Keep eligibility denominators consistent

slides.title: Repeated observations and clustering
points: Account for multiple measurements per participant or site
Distinguish patients from visits or procedures
Choose uncertainty estimates that respect dependence

slides.title: History and secular trends
points: External events or background changes may explain the difference
Record contemporaneous policies and service disruptions
Recognize that one pre-post contrast cannot separate these effects

slides.title: Maturation and regression to the mean
points: Outcomes may change naturally with time
Extreme baseline values tend to be less extreme on repeat measurement
Consider whether eligibility was triggered by unusually poor performance

slides.title: Testing and instrumentation effects
points: Participants may respond differently after repeated testing
Instruments, assessors or definitions may change
Examine these possibilities before interpreting improvement

slides.title: Missing follow-up and attrition
points: Compare observed participants with those lost to follow-up
Report unavailable outcomes rather than treating them as unchanged
Assess sensitivity to plausible missing-data mechanisms

slides.title: Worked change example
points: Hypothetical attendance rises from 60% to 75%
The absolute observed change is 15 percentage points
This difference alone cannot isolate the reminder system's effect

slides.title: Ethics and reporting
points: Follow applicable approvals for intervention delivery and research data
Report eligibility, implementation, windows and missingness
Present estimates with uncertainty and explicit design limitations

slides.title: Strengths, limitations and takeaways
points: Simple and useful for documenting local change
Highly vulnerable to time-related alternative explanations
Discuss adding a comparator or multiple observations before and after

slides.title: References and further reading
points: Cochrane Handbook, Chapter 25: Assessing risk of bias in a non-randomized study. https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-25
JBI Critical Appraisal Tools. https://jbi.global/critical-appraisal-tools

slides.title: Controlled before-and-after study
points: Compare pre-post changes between an intervention group and a nonrandomized comparison group
Core concepts, study planning, analysis and interpretation
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple design schematic

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and structure of the design
Plan sampling, measurement and appropriate analysis
Assess bias, interpretation, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and structure
points: Measure outcomes in intervention and comparison groups before and after implementation
Allocation is not randomized
Use the comparison group to assess background changes

slides.title: Purpose and design scope
points: Estimate change associated with an intervention beyond a comparison group's change
Examine assumptions supporting that contrast
Recognize overlap with nonrandomized intervention studies

slides.title: When the design fits
points: Use for service or policy changes when randomization is impractical
Seek a plausible contemporaneous comparison
Consider whether longer time-series data are available

slides.title: Formulating the question
points: Specify intervention, comparison, population and time windows
Define the main outcome and desired effect
State the intended causal contrast and assumptions

slides.title: Illustrative research problem
points: Hypothetical example: a reminder system introduced at one clinic but not another
Measure attendance before and after at both clinics
Assess differences in populations and background trends

slides.title: Unit of allocation and analysis
points: Identify whether interventions are assigned to clinics, wards or individuals
Distinguish allocation units from outcome observations
Account for clustered data in planning and analysis

slides.title: Selecting the comparison group
points: Choose a group with similar determinants of the outcome
Align calendar periods and eligibility
Avoid selection based only on matching one baseline mean

slides.title: Documenting nonrandom allocation
points: Explain why one group received the intervention
Identify decision-makers and allocation criteria
Consider how those criteria also predict outcomes

slides.title: Baseline comparability
points: Describe differences in demographics, services and outcomes
Assess determinants relevant to the research question
Avoid interpreting nonsignificant baseline tests as proof of equivalence

slides.title: Intervention and co-interventions
points: Specify content, timing and implementation fidelity
Record other changes in both groups
Identify spillover and contamination

slides.title: Measurement schedules
points: Collect comparable pre and post data in both groups
Use common windows and outcome definitions
Obtain additional pre-intervention periods when feasible

slides.title: Sampling and power
points: Plan using the unit of allocation, effect and expected variability
Account for clustering and repeated measurement
Large patient counts cannot compensate for very few independent sites

slides.title: Outcome definitions and denominators
points: Use consistent numerator and denominator rules across groups and time
Verify coding stability
Record population turnover and missing observations

slides.title: Difference-in-differences logic
points: Compare the intervention group's change with the comparison group's change
Define the interaction contrast as the target estimate where appropriate
Explain the counterfactual interpretation

slides.title: Parallel trends and related assumptions
points: Assume untreated outcome changes would have been comparable, conditional on the chosen framework
Inspect pre-intervention trends when available
Recognize that similar baseline values do not establish parallel trends

slides.title: Statistical analysis
points: Use regression suited to the outcome and dependence structure
Estimate group-by-period effects when that matches the estimand
Report absolute or relative effects with uncertainty

slides.title: Clustering and repeated measures
points: Account for correlation within sites and within participants
Choose methods suited to the number of independent units
Explain small-cluster uncertainty limitations

slides.title: Confounding and differential changes
points: Consider time-varying changes affecting groups differently
Adjust measured factors using a causal rationale
A comparator does not eliminate all confounding

slides.title: Contamination and population shifts
points: Check whether comparison participants receive elements of the intervention
Assess turnover or altered referral pathways
Explain how these changes affect the contrast

slides.title: Worked difference-in-differences example
points: Hypothetical attendance changes from 60% to 75% in the intervention group and 65% to 70% in controls
The difference in changes is 10 percentage points
Causal interpretation still requires credible assumptions

slides.title: Sensitivity analyses and ethics
points: Examine alternative windows, comparators and outcome definitions
Test sensitivity to site differences and missingness
Follow applicable intervention and data-review requirements

slides.title: Reporting, strengths and takeaways
points: Report allocation, comparison selection, pre-post measurements and assumptions
Explain clustering, concurrent changes and implementation
Discuss whether the comparator credibly represents untreated change

slides.title: References and further reading
points: Cochrane Handbook, Chapter 25: Assessing risk of bias in a non-randomized study. https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-25
Cochrane EPOC: study-design guidance. https://epoc.cochrane.org/sites/epoc.cochrane.org/files/uploads/Resources-for-authors2017/what_study_designs_should_be_included_in_an_epoc_review.pdf

slides.title: Interrupted time-series study
points: Estimate changes in outcome level or trend following a clearly timed intervention
Core concepts, study planning, analysis and interpretation
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple design schematic

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and structure of the design
Plan sampling, measurement and appropriate analysis
Assess bias, interpretation, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and temporal structure
points: Use repeated outcome observations before and after an intervention
Specify when the intervention occurred
Compare post-intervention observations with a modeled counterfactual trend

slides.title: ITS versus a simple pre-post study
points: ITS explicitly models the existing outcome trend
Multiple observations allow evaluation of level and slope changes
A single before and after measurement cannot establish a time-series trend

slides.title: When the design fits
points: Use for policies or service changes introduced at a defined time
Require sufficiently frequent and reliable observations
Consider control series when contemporaneous changes threaten inference

slides.title: Formulating the question
points: Specify intervention, outcome, population and expected timing of response
Define level change, trend change or another impact pattern
Prespecify the main effect model where possible

slides.title: Illustrative research problem
points: Hypothetical example: monthly clinic attendance after reminder-system rollout
Examine existing trends and calendar effects
Avoid attributing an unrelated seasonal rise to implementation

slides.title: Defining the interruption
points: Document announcement, rollout and actual implementation dates
Consider anticipation, phased implementation and lagged effects
Explain which date or transition period the model uses

slides.title: Selecting outcome data
points: Use consistent repeated measurements with stable definitions
Check denominators for rates or proportions
Record changes in reporting systems and coverage

slides.title: Frequency and observation window
points: Choose intervals suited to the outcome and expected effect
Include enough pre and post observations to model relevant patterns
Avoid treating a minimal eligibility threshold as evidence of sufficient power

slides.title: Sample size and power
points: Consider number of time points, variability, autocorrelation and expected effect
Account for seasonality and model complexity
More participants within one point do not replace adequate temporal information

slides.title: Exploratory visualization
points: Plot all observations and the intervention date
Inspect missing periods, outliers and background patterns
Keep exploratory impressions separate from prespecified inference

slides.title: Defining the impact model
points: Compare immediate level change, slope change, delayed response and temporary effects
Use substantive knowledge to choose the primary model
Avoid selecting the model solely for statistical significance

slides.title: Segmented regression
points: Model baseline level and pre-intervention trend
Add terms for the intervention and time after intervention when appropriate
Match the link function to the outcome

slides.title: Interpreting level change
points: Describe the immediate departure from the projected counterfactual
State the scale and timing of the estimate
Consider whether immediate change is plausible for the intervention

slides.title: Interpreting slope change
points: Describe the post-intervention change in trend relative to baseline
Distinguish trend change from the total effect at a later time
Report units per interval clearly

slides.title: Estimating effects at a chosen horizon
points: Combine relevant model terms for the prespecified time point
Compare predicted observed and counterfactual outcomes
Include uncertainty in the derived contrast

slides.title: Autocorrelation
points: Successive observations may have correlated errors
Check temporal dependence with appropriate diagnostics
Use models or error structures that address relevant autocorrelation

slides.title: Seasonality and nonlinear patterns
points: Model recurring calendar effects when relevant
Assess whether a linear trend is defensible
Avoid overfitting with too few time points

slides.title: Time-varying confounding
points: Record policies, disruptions and other interventions near the interruption
Consider whether they can explain the observed change
Recognize that an uncontrolled series cannot separate every simultaneous event

slides.title: Controlled ITS
points: Add an appropriate unexposed outcome or population series
Compare changes while accounting for baseline differences in trends
State assumptions about shared external influences and contamination

slides.title: Model checks and sensitivity analyses
points: Inspect residuals, outliers and alternative plausible timing assumptions
Test sensitivity to transition periods and influential points
Report planned and exploratory analyses distinctly

slides.title: Worked interpretation and ethics
points: Hypothetical model suggests an immediate 8-percentage-point attendance increase with no clear slope change
Discuss uncertainty, seasonality and concurrent events
Follow applicable data-use and intervention-review requirements

slides.title: Reporting, strengths and takeaways
points: Report dates, observation counts, impact model and dependence adjustments
Present observed and counterfactual trajectories with uncertainty
Discuss why a plausible time trend is essential to inference

slides.title: References and further reading
points: Lopez Bernal J, Cummins S, Gasparrini A. Interrupted time series regression for the evaluation of public health interventions: a tutorial. International Journal of Epidemiology. 2017;46:348-355. https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw098
Cochrane Handbook, Chapter 25: Assessing risk of bias in a non-randomized study. https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-25

slides.title: Nonrandomized controlled trial
points: Evaluate an investigator-assigned intervention against a comparator without random allocation
Core concepts, study planning, analysis and interpretation
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple design schematic

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and structure of the design
Plan sampling, measurement and appropriate analysis
Assess bias, interpretation, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and allocation
points: Investigators assign intervention and comparator groups without randomization
Measure subsequent outcomes under a planned protocol
Distinguish investigator assignment from observing routine treatment choices

slides.title: Relationship to other designs
points: A cohort may observe exposure without assigning it
Controlled before-after designs include measurements before and after in both groups
Trial and quasi-experimental labels can overlap, so describe actual procedures

slides.title: When nonrandomized trials are used
points: Consider logistical, operational or preference constraints
Explain why randomization was not feasible
Assess whether the remaining design can answer the intervention question

slides.title: Formulating the question
points: Specify population, intervention, comparator, outcome and time horizon
Define the intended treatment effect
Identify the decision point at which groups are assigned

slides.title: Illustrative research problem
points: Hypothetical example: clinicians assign two patient-education approaches by clinic schedule
Evaluate later knowledge or attendance
Examine whether schedule and clinic differences predict outcomes

slides.title: Protocol and analysis planning
points: Specify procedures and outcomes before enrollment
Prespecify confounders and analysis methods
Use appropriate registration or public protocol practices where applicable

slides.title: Eligibility and recruitment
points: Apply comparable criteria to both groups
Recruit before outcome development where possible
Record preferences and reasons for participation or refusal

slides.title: Nonrandom allocation mechanism
points: Describe clinician choice, location, time or other assignment rules
Avoid calling alternation or date-based assignment truly random
Assess predictability and selection opportunities

slides.title: Selecting the comparator
points: Define usual care, active treatment or another appropriate comparator
Ensure contemporaneous and comparable follow-up
Explain why the comparator answers the intended question

slides.title: Baseline measurement
points: Record prognostic characteristics before treatment assignment or initiation as appropriate
Measure confounders with consistent procedures
Evaluate overlap between groups

slides.title: Intervention delivery and adherence
points: Specify intervention content, dose and delivery
Document adherence, crossover and co-interventions
Distinguish assigned treatment from treatment received

slides.title: Blinding and outcome assessment
points: Blind assessors or analysts where feasible
Use objective or standardized outcomes
Explain when participants or staff cannot be blinded

slides.title: Outcome definitions and follow-up
points: Prespecify primary and secondary outcomes
Align time zero and assessment windows
Avoid preferential outcome assessment in one group

slides.title: Sample size and precision
points: Base planning on the intended effect, event frequency and variability
Include expected attrition and clustering
Consider loss of information from poor overlap or matching

slides.title: Confounding and prognostic imbalance
points: Allocation may depend on factors that also affect outcomes
Identify confounding by indication or preference
Explain why baseline adjustment is central but not sufficient

slides.title: Regression adjustment
points: Choose outcome models that estimate the intended contrast
Adjust prespecified prognostic confounders
Avoid controlling for post-treatment mediators without a clear estimand

slides.title: Propensity score methods
points: Consider matching, weighting or stratification when assumptions are credible
Assess overlap and covariate balance after adjustment
Explain that these methods do not resolve unmeasured confounding

slides.title: Defining the analysis population
points: Specify assignment-based, as-treated or per-protocol contrasts
Explain how crossover and adherence affect interpretation
Avoid treating assignment-based analysis as restoring randomization

slides.title: Missing data and attrition
points: Report outcome completeness by group and reasons for loss
Use methods with stated assumptions
Examine sensitivity to informative missingness

slides.title: Worked interpretation example
points: Hypothetical adjusted analysis favors one education strategy
Examine whether motivated patients were preferentially assigned to it
Separate an adjusted association from a credible causal estimate

slides.title: Ethics, harms and risk of bias
points: Obtain appropriate approvals and informed consent for trial procedures
Monitor harms in both groups
Assess allocation, confounding, measurement and missingness systematically

slides.title: Reporting, strengths and takeaways
points: Describe nonrandom allocation and its rationale clearly
Report protocol, flow, adjustments, adherence and harms
Discuss residual confounding and when randomization would strengthen inference

slides.title: References and further reading
points: Cochrane Handbook, Chapter 25: Assessing risk of bias in a non-randomized study. https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-25
JBI Critical Appraisal Tools. https://jbi.global/critical-appraisal-tools

slides.title: Randomized controlled trial (RCT)
points: Estimate intervention effects using randomized allocation and a prespecified trial protocol
Core concepts, study planning, analysis and interpretation
slides.visual: Title slide with a simple design schematic

slides.title: Learning objectives
points: Explain the purpose and structure of the design
Plan sampling, measurement and appropriate analysis
Assess bias, interpretation, ethics and reporting

slides.title: Definition and purpose
points: Randomly assign eligible participants or groups to interventions
Compare outcomes under a prespecified protocol
Use randomization to support exchangeability on average, not guarantee identical groups

slides.title: When an RCT fits
points: Use when intervention assignment is ethical and feasible
Ensure the comparator addresses a meaningful question
Assess recruitment, follow-up and operational feasibility

slides.title: Formulating the trial question
points: Specify population, intervention, comparator, outcomes and time horizon
Define the estimand, including handling of intercurrent events
Connect the question with clinically meaningful decisions

slides.title: Illustrative research problem
points: Hypothetical example: randomized reminder messages versus usual appointment communication
Evaluate attendance at a defined time
Prespecify harms, burden and secondary outcomes

slides.title: Protocol and registration
points: Use SPIRIT 2025 to guide protocol reporting
Register the trial prospectively according to applicable requirements
Finalize the analysis plan before outcome-driven changes

slides.title: Common trial structures
points: Compare parallel, crossover, cluster and factorial structures
Choose according to intervention, carryover and contamination risks
Explain structure-specific analysis requirements

slides.title: Eligibility and recruitment
points: Define criteria that balance safety and applicability
Recruit without knowledge of upcoming allocation
Record screening and reasons for exclusion

slides.title: Comparator and intervention definition
points: Specify usual care, placebo or an active comparator
Describe intervention delivery sufficiently for replication
Keep co-interventions and permitted care clear

slides.title: Random sequence generation
points: Use a genuinely random allocation method
Describe blocking or stratification where applied
Keep prediction of upcoming assignments difficult

slides.title: Allocation concealment
points: Prevent foreknowledge of the next assignment during enrollment
Consider centralized or securely implemented allocation
Distinguish concealment from blinding after assignment

slides.title: Blinding
points: Identify which participants, staff, assessors or analysts are blinded
Explain how blinding is maintained or why it is infeasible
Assess susceptibility of outcomes to knowledge of allocation

slides.title: Sample size and power
points: Specify primary outcome, effect size, error rates and variability assumptions
Account for attrition, clustering or repeated measurement
Choose assumptions grounded in the clinical question

slides.title: Primary and secondary outcomes
points: Prespecify outcome definitions and assessment times
Limit multiplicity and explain the hierarchy of outcomes
Distinguish patient-important outcomes from surrogates

slides.title: Follow-up, adherence and intercurrent events
points: Plan consistent assessment in all groups
Record adherence, discontinuation, rescue therapy and crossover
Handle these events according to the estimand and analysis plan

slides.title: Baseline characteristics
points: Describe prognostic factors and group composition
Recognize chance imbalances can occur after randomization
Avoid routine significance testing as proof of successful randomization

slides.title: Primary statistical analysis
points: Use an outcome model aligned with the estimand and design
Include prespecified covariate adjustment where justified
Report effect estimates with confidence intervals

slides.title: Intention-to-treat principle
points: Analyze participants according to randomized assignment for the relevant assignment-based effect
Do not exclude participants solely for nonadherence
Explain missing outcomes rather than implying ITT solves missingness

slides.title: Per-protocol and supplementary analyses
points: Define adherence and protocol deviations in advance
Recognize potential selection bias from naive exclusions
Use suitable methods and distinguish supplementary from primary conclusions

slides.title: Absolute and relative treatment effects
points: Report measures suited to binary, continuous or time-to-event outcomes
Pair relative contrasts with absolute effects when useful
Distinguish hazard ratios, risk ratios and risk differences

slides.title: Worked effect example
points: Hypothetical event risks are 10% with intervention and 15% with control at one year
Risk ratio is 0.67 and absolute risk reduction is 5 percentage points
NNT is 20 over that horizon if the event is undesirable and the contrast is appropriate

slides.title: Safety, ethics and trial monitoring
points: Require meaningful consent, appropriate review and a defensible treatment comparison
Prespecify harm collection and monitoring suited to risk
Plan interim decisions without ignoring multiplicity or operational bias

slides.title: Reporting, strengths and takeaways
points: Use CONSORT 2025 and relevant design-specific extensions
Report participant flow, outcomes, uncertainty, harms and deviations
Discuss remaining risks from attrition, nonadherence and limited applicability

slides.title: References and further reading
points: SPIRIT 2025 and CONSORT 2025: randomized trial protocol and reporting guidance. https://www.consort-spirit.org/
Published statements and explanation documents. https://www.consort-spirit.org/published-statements
